History: The house was built in 1861 by prominent merchant Ivan Konstantinov, the father of Aleko Konstantinov. Aleko was born in the house in 1863 and lived there during his youth. Following his assassination in 1897, the property was transferred to the Svishtov municipality. It was officially opened to the public as a memorial museum in 1926, establishing it as one of the oldest literary museums in Bulgaria.
Architecture: The building is a prime example of mid-19th century Bulgarian National Revival residential architecture. The symmetrical, two-story structure reflects the high social and economic status of the Svishtov merchant class. The preserved interior features richly decorated carved wooden ceilings and authentic period furnishings, including original Viennese furniture imported by the Konstantinov family.
Exhibitions: The museum's collection spans multiple rooms detailing the author's life, literary contributions, and civic activism. The exhibits include original manuscripts, personal correspondence, photographs, and early editions of his defining works, such as 'Bay Ganyo' and 'To Chicago and Back'. The upper floor meticulously recreates the domestic environment of a wealthy Bulgarian family during the late 19th century.
Notable Relics: The exhibition includes the clothes Konstantinov was wearing on the day of his assassination near the village of Radilovo. The most macabre and notable artifact on display is the author's preserved heart, kept in a glass container, which still exhibits the fatal bullet wound.
Cultural Legacy: Beyond his literary satire, Konstantinov is recognized as the founder of the organized tourist movement in Bulgaria, having initiated the mass ascent of Cherni Vrah in 1895. The museum serves as a monument to this legacy and is officially listed as one of the 100 Tourist Sites of Bulgaria.
